body:
Current requirement:
> V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary, using the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive. Note that X-Frame-Options is **now** obsolete.

Proposal to move the "now" from
> Note that X-Frame-Options is now obsolete.

Or just use:
> Note that X-Frame-Options header field is obsoleted.

---

edit: "using the Content-Security-Policy frame-ancestors directive"

This part should also be polished to say clearly, that Content-Security-Policy is header field and frame-ancestors it is it's directive.

comments.body:
Suggest:

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary, using the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field. The X-Frame-Options header field can also be used but only with the "DENY" or "SOMEORIGIN" directives.._"

It appears that ALLOW-FROM directive is obsolete but the rest of the header is not.

https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP2/#frame-ancestors-and-frame-options

> The frame-ancestors directive **obsoletes the X-Frame-Options header**. If a resource has both policies, the frame-ancestors policy SHOULD be enforced and the X-Frame-Options policy SHOULD be ignored.

Excellent point :)

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field to ensure that it cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. This directive replaces the X-Frame-Options header field which is obsolete and is no longer to be used for this purpose._"

> This directive replaces the X-Frame-Options header field which is obsolete and is no longer to be used for this purpose.

this seems a bit wordy and "_is no longer to be used for this purpose_" kind of hints that there is some other purpose for the header field (that I'm not aware of), so I prefer my initial proposal:
> Note that X-Frame-Options header field is obsoleted.

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field to ensure that it cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. This directive replaces the X-Frame-Options header field **which is considered obsolete**._"

If a company uses XFO and not the CSP directive, do they fail this requirement?

> If a company uses XFO and not the CSP directive, do they fail this requirement?

In practice from an attacker point of view, if I can not do UI redress attack (such as clickjacking), then it does not matter what was used against it.

In practice from a developer point of view, I want to make future-proof solutions and although x-frame-options provides defense in practice today, I don't know when and if it will be deprecated from browsers.

Personally I report this kind of stuff as "info" risk - defense at the moment exists, but be aware of the situation.

Ok so I think we may have gone in a circle as I think that needs to be clear (changes indicated compared to current state in Github):

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default, and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary, using the **frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field**. Whilst also providing protection, the X-Frame-Options header field is  ~~now~~ considered obsolete **so new applications should not use it and existing applications should plan to migrate away from it.**_"
and I still think the last part is not necessary and is a cheat sheet content
Either we don't mention how to do this or we have to mention the possible mechanisms that allow passing this requirement.

> and I still think the last part is not necessary and is a cheat sheet content

More precisely I addressed this part:
> so new applications should not use it and existing applications should plan to migrate away from it

I need to be able to read the requirement, see an app using XFO and understand whether this is a pass or a fail.

Without saying "so new applications should not use it and existing applications should plan to migrate away from it" I don't think this is clear.

An alternative is just to say this and leave all implementation detail to cheat sheets or section text:

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default (such as inside an iframe), and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary._"

> I need to be able to read the requirement, see an app using XFO and understand whether this is a pass or a fail.

The answer is explained here: https://github.com/OWASP/ASVS/issues/2757#issuecomment-2747101836

> V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default (such as inside an iframe), and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary.

I think to build a requirement, this is the correct way to do it - asking to mitigate vulnerability, not asking precise HTTP response header.

But, it still must contain CSP frame-ancestors, it still need to say, that XFO is obsoleted. 

~~Also, if we consider, that there are alternative solutions how to handle it, maybe we need to move it away from 50.3 section, and if we do that, we need to do the same for some other requirement (such as 50.3.4), and then, maybe we need to re-organize entire V50.~~

That "remove "now"" escalated quickly.

I think the only legit protections would be one of the above options so I don't really want to start reorganising everything.

Can we go with this and mention the relevant headers in section text?

"_V50.3.5 [MODIFIED, MOVED FROM 14.4.7] Verify that the content of the web application cannot be embedded in a third-party site by default (such as inside an iframe), and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary._"

I think with that proposal, do solve one problem you replace it with larger one.

With XFO - we can not say you are safe and we can not say you are not. We may say that _today_ you are ok, but this is not future-proof solution for a requirement. That is why my clear proposal to point it out, that XFO is obsolete.

Rethinking about it - CSP frame-ancestors is must have to use to be sure that you satisfy the requirement.

Additionally, I think we need to remove "in a third-party site", because allowing embedding resources by it's own application (same-origin scope) provides nice bypasses of CSP and other tricks with UI in an HTML injection condition.

> Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete.

Note that the proposal has a wider scope than "clickjacking" - as clickjacking is a valid problem only when some clickable UI functionality is exposed to a third party, but the proposed requirement asks to disallow any embedding. As it also covers clickjacking vector we don't need to have a separate one.
So is XFO a pass or a fail?

We could say:

"_Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete **and may not be relied upon**._"

If it was written
> With XFO - we can not say you are safe and we can not say you are not. We may say that today you are ok, but this is not future-proof solution for a requirement. That is why my clear proposal to point it out, that XFO is obsolete.

and asked
>So is XFO a pass or a fail?

I have nothing polite to say :)

---

One more tiny proposal change to the last one:
> Verify that the web application uses the frame-ancestors directive of the Content-Security-Policy header field **for every HTTP response** to ensure that it cannot be embedded by default and that embedding of specific resources is allowed only when necessary. Note that the X-Frame-Options header field, although supported by browsers, is obsolete and may not be relied upon.

> I have nothing polite to say :)

You miss my point. if the answer is not clear in the requirement then that is the problem. 

Either way, I think we now have agreement on wording so I opened #2771

Frame ancestors and XFO are both incomplete and often bypassable ways to stop clickjacking. The deeper defenses I see are detecting mouse movements and similar. You can ignore this if you want, I know we are close to release, but again, this requirement is not fully effective against clickjacking anymore.
The requirement is against 3rd party embedding and covers that part of the clickjacking. If the clickjacking is done using some other techniques, it is not subject to this requirement.
I think the question is, aside from the headers above, are there clear requirements that we should also be asking developers to implement? If so, please open a follow-up issue @jmanico
